tip: Μου φαινόταν (mou fenótan) = it seemed to me; the ongoing past form, used for an impression that lasted.
Μου έκανε εντύπωση (mou ékane endíposi) flips the roles: the quiet 'made an impression to me'. You're the landing spot, as in μου λείπει (mou lípi = I miss it).
Doubling an adverb is how Greek stretches it: σιγά σιγά (sighá sighá) = little by little. Same pattern in λίγο λίγο (lígho lígho = bit by bit).
Κάνω παρέα με (káno paréa me) is literally 'I make company with' – in Greek, hanging out is company you make, not time you spend.
A circle of friends needs no 'of' word: κύκλο καλών φίλων (kíklo kalón fílon) – the -ων endings carry it. Reaching for από (apó) is the English reflex.
Μέσω (méso) = via/through: μέσω βίντεο (méso vídeo) = over video, a compact and slightly formal alternative to με (me).
Μου λείπει (mou lípi) = I miss; literally 'it is missing to me', so the thing you miss is what the verb follows.
Οι δικοί μου (i dhikí mou) = my folks; here στους δικούς μου (stus dhikús mou) = to my folks. Warm and everyday.
Παρόλο που (parólo pu) = even though, and it's followed by a plain statement verb: μου έλειπε (mou élipe = I missed it).
Μπερδεύτηκα (berdéftika) is literally 'I got tangled up', the everyday verb for getting confused. Χάνομαι (khánome = I get lost) doesn't work here.
Μόλις (mólis) has two jobs: 'as soon as' – μόλις προσγειώθηκα (mólis prosyióthika = as soon as I landed) – and 'just/barely'. Context decides which.
Greek days are 'small', not short: οι μέρες ήταν τόσο μικρές (i méres ítan tóso mikrés). Κοντή (kondí = short) is for physical length; days run μικρή/μεγάλη (mikrí/megháli).
Κάνω υπομονή (káno ipomoní) is literally 'do patience' = be patient; here έκανα υπομονή (ékana ipomoní) = I was patient.
Καιρός (kerós) means both 'time' and 'weather': με τον καιρό (me ton keró) uses the time sense, 'with time' = over time.
Όσο (óso) + a past verb runs two changes in parallel: όσο περνούσε ο καιρός (óso pernúse o kerós) = as time went by, and the feeling shifted with it.
Greek takes decisions instead of making them: πήρα την απόφαση (píra tin apófasi) = literally 'I took the decision'. Κάνω (káno = make) is the wrong verb here.
Με τίποτα (me típota) is literally 'with nothing': δεν θα άλλαζα... με τίποτα (dhen tha álaza... me típota) = I wouldn't trade it for anything.
Παρά (pará) = 'than' when two matching phrases are compared: περισσότερα... παρά (perissótera... pará), about myself than about the country. Από (apó) compares plain nouns.
Θα (tha) + a past verb = 'would': θα το ξανάκανα (tha to ksanákana) = I'd do it again. The same θα that builds the future turns past forms into 'would'.
Πως (pos) and ότι (óti) both work as 'that' after belief verbs: πιστεύω πως (pistévo pos) = πιστεύω ότι (pistévo óti), same meaning either way.
Έχεις δίκιο (ékhis dhíkio) = you're right, literally 'you have right'.
Κάθετα (kátheta) is literally 'vertically': διαφωνώ κάθετα (dhiafonó kátheta) = 'I disagree vertically', the Greek way of saying flatly, completely.
Στα (sta) + an adjective in -ά makes an adverb phrase: στα σοβαρά (sta sovará) = seriously, στα κρυφά (sta krifá) = secretly.
Ας (as) + verb = 'let's': ας υποθέσουμε (as ipothésume) = let's suppose. Swap the verb and ας still carries it – ας πάμε (as páme) = let's go.
Τα βρουν (ta vrun) hides a filler 'them': τα βρίσκω (ta vrísko = literally I find them) means to come to terms. That 'them' points at nothing; it's part of the idiom.
Greek flips the English order: άσπρο μαύρο (áspro mávro) is literally 'white black', not black and white. Same oversimplification, opposite color order.
Στο ίδιο τσουβάλι (sto ídhio tsuváli) = literally 'in the same sack'; putting everything in it = lumping it all together.
Μπορεί να (borí na) = it may/might. In this sense μπορεί stays in that one fixed form, whoever is involved.
Εν πάση περιπτώσει (en pási periptósi) = in any case; a frozen ancient phrase – modern Greek uses σε (se) rather than εν (en) outside set expressions like this.
Πολυλογώ (poliloghó) is literally 'I many-word': πολυ- (poli-) glues onto the verb. Για να μην τα πολυλογώ (ya na min ta poliloghó) = to keep it short.
